 distinct byte addresses.

Each address bit doubles the number of distinct addresses.
qs.rel: Address width arithmetic: A address bits give 2^A addressable units; capacity = 2^A x unit size. Neighbours: 10 bits = 1K, 16 bits = 64K, 20 bits = 1M, 32 bits = 4G locations.

qs.stem: How many memory references are required to fetch an operand in indirect addressing?
qs.sol: In indirect addressing, the instruction contains a memory address that points to the location of the operand. The first memory reference is used to fetch this address. The second memory reference is then used to fetch the actual operand from the address obtained in the first step. Therefore, two memory references are required.
qs.rel: Indirect addressing: first reference reads the pointer, second reads the operand (two references). Direct = one, immediate/register = zero. Multi-level indirection is possible but slower; useful for pointers and tables.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are true about components of CPU? 
(i) A CPU has only 2 components. 
(ii) Control Unit is a CPU’s component.
qs.sol: A Central Processing Unit typically contains three main functional units: the Control Unit, Arithmetic Logic Unit, and Registers. Statement (i) is incorrect because it claims there are only two components. Statement (ii) is correct as the Control Unit manages instruction execution within the processor structure.
qs.rel: CPU components: ALU, control unit and registers (three, not two). Some books describe CPU as control unit + datapath. Memory and I/O are outside the CPU in von Neumann model.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a common field found in instruction formats?
qs.sol:
An instruction format commonly has an opcode and may include an address and addressing-mode field.

A general sign field is not a standard common field.
qs.rel: Instruction format fields are opcode, address field(s) and mode field. Sign bit belongs to data representation, not format. Also instruction length, number of address fields, and register field vary by design.

qs.stem: Which of the following addressing modes stores the operand in the instruction?
qs.sol: Immediate addressing mode stores the operand directly within the instruction itself, embedding the data value in the code rather than referencing a memory address or register.
qs.rel: Immediate mode puts the operand in the instruction (no memory reference), useful for constants. Implied mode has operand implicit; register mode keeps it in a register. Direct needs one memory access.

qs.stem: Which of the following algorithms refers to displacement addressing mode?
qs.sol:
Displacement addressing forms the effective address by adding a displacement A to the contents of a register R: EA = A + (R).

The effective address sums a fixed displacement and register contents.
qs.rel: Displacement addressing: EA = A + (R). Relative uses PC, indexed uses index register, base-register uses base register. Direct EA = A, indirect EA = (A), register indirect EA = (R).

qs.stem:
To which of the following categories does the given instruction belong?

LOAD    A    AC←M[A]
A

One-Address Instructions

B

Two-Address Instructions

C

Three-Address Instructions

D

Zero-Address Instructions
qs.sol:
The instruction names one explicit memory address, A.

The accumulator AC is implicit in AC←M[A], so this is a one-address instruction.
qs.rel: Address-count classification: LOAD A has one explicit address with accumulator implicit (one-address). ADD R1,A,B is three-address; zero-address uses stack. Two-address forms like MOV R1,A overwrite one source.

qs.stem: Which of the following Instruction format use an implied accumulator (AC) register for all data manipulation?
qs.sol: One-address instructions commonly use an implied accumulator register for data manipulation.
qs.rel: Single-accumulator (one-address) organisation uses implied AC for ALU operations: LOAD, ADD, STORE. Contrast general-register (two or three address) and stack (zero address, PUSH/POP).

qs.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of a RISC processor?
qs.sol:
Concept

An instruction set specifies the operations a processor can perform and how operands are represented. Simpler, regular operations reduce the work needed to decode and execute each instruction.

Pipelining overlaps stages of successive instructions. Instruction latency and the rate of completing instructions are different measures, so a design goal must be distinguished from a universal timing guarantee.

Application

RISC means Reduced Instruction Set Computer. Its classical design uses simple operations, regular instruction formats and relatively few addressing modes to keep the control logic simple. …
qs.rel: RISC characteristics: few simple fixed-length instructions, single-cycle execution, load/store architecture, many registers, hardwired control, pipelining. CISC has many instructions, variable length, many addressing modes.

qs.stem: Which of the following elements of a machine instruction specifies the operation to be performed?
qs.sol:
The operation code field specifies the action that the machine instruction performs.

The opcode identifies the operation to execute.
qs.rel: Elements of a machine instruction: opcode, source operand reference, result operand reference, next-instruction reference. Opcode of n bits gives 2^n operations. Mnemonic is the symbolic opcode name.

qs.stem: Which of the following is a correct statement about RAM?

opts.A: It stands for Read Access Memory.
opts.C: It can be directly accessed by the CPU.
opts.D: Its speed is greater than Cache memory.

qs.sol:
Concept

Random access means a memory location can be selected by its address without reading all preceding locations. Volatility describes whether stored data survives removal of power.

In the conventional computer memory hierarchy, the processor uses main memory for active programs and data, while cache holds nearby copies to reduce access time.

Application

A running program places its instructions and working data in main RAM. A load or store instruction identifies an address in that memory.

The CPU issues the memory request through the memory system. A cache hit may supply a load; on a miss, the requested data is fetched from main RAM through the memory controller. …
qs.rel: RAM: random access, volatile, directly accessible by CPU, read/write. SRAM is faster than DRAM. ROM is non-volatile. Do not confuse random access (constant time) with sequential and direct access.

qs.stem: In CPU, which of the following type of register is required by the control unit and contains the instruction currently being executed?
qs.sol: The instruction register holds the instruction currently being executed by the CPU control unit.
qs.rel: Instruction register holds the instruction being executed; the control unit decodes it. Neighbours: PC (next address), MAR (memory address), MDR (data), accumulator (ALU operand and result).

qs.stem:
State whether the following statements are true or false.

(i) With one-address instructions, the programmer generally has available only one general-purpose register, the accumulator.

(ii) Zero-address instructions are applicable to a special memory organization called a stack.
qs.sol: Statement (i) is true because one-address instructions implicitly use the accumulator as an operand, limiting available general-purpose registers. Statement (ii) is true because zero-address instructions operate on a stack where operands are implicitly accessed via push and pop operations without explicit memory addresses.
qs.rel: One-address machines have one accumulator; zero-address machines use a stack with implicit operands (postfix evaluation). Be ready to write code for (A+B)*(C+D) in 0-, 1-, 2- and 3-address forms.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are true about control unit?
 I. It manages and coordinate the entire computer system.
 II. It does not perform any actual processing  on data.
qs.sol:
Step 1: The control unit is responsible for managing and coordinating all components of the computer system, including the CPU, memory, and input/output devices. This makes statement I correct.

Step 2: The control unit does not perform actual data processing such as arithmetic or logical operations. These tasks are handled by the ALU. Therefore, statement II is also correct.

Step 3: Since both statements I and II are accurate descriptions of the control unit's functions, the correct choice is the one that includes both.
qs.rel: Control unit coordinates all components and performs no actual data processing. Neighbours: it generates control signals via hardwired logic or microprogram, uses clock for timing, and interprets the opcode.

qs.stem: Which of the following addressing modes does NOT store the operand in the memory?
qs.sol: Implied addressing defines the operand implicitly within the instruction or a specific register, avoiding memory access. In contrast, modes like Register Indirect and Memory Indirect require retrieving operands from main memory locations to function correctly.
qs.rel: Implied addressing has the operand built into the opcode (for example CMA, stack ops), so no memory operand. Register indirect, indirect and relative modes all reach memory. Immediate and register modes also avoid memory.

qs.stem: Which of the following are the three forms of memory typically, volatile and use semiconductor technology?
qs.sol:
Registers, main memory, and cache commonly use volatile semiconductor storage.

Secondary and auxiliary storage are generally nonvolatile.
qs.rel: Registers, cache and main memory are volatile semiconductor memories. Secondary storage (disk, tape) is magnetic/optical and non-volatile. Semiconductor non-volatile examples: ROM, flash, SSD.

qs.stem: In stack organisation of a CPU, the register that holds the address of stack is referred to as ____.
qs.sol:
The stack pointer register holds the address of the current top of the stack and changes on push and pop.

It stores the stack-top address.
qs.rel: Stack pointer holds the address of the stack top and is decremented/incremented on push/pop. Stack is LIFO; used for subroutine return addresses, interrupts, and postfix evaluation. Overflow and underflow are error conditions.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a CPU organisation type with respect to instruction formats?
qs.sol:
Accumulator, general-register and stack organisations are established CPU instruction organisations.

Queue organisation is not the usual CPU organisation in this classification.
qs.rel: CPU organisations by instruction format: single accumulator, general register, stack. Queue organisation is not one. Stack uses zero-address, accumulator one-address, general register two- or three-address.

qs.stem: Which of the following is defined as the memory address obtained from the computation dictated by a given addressing mode?
qs.sol:
An addressing mode specifies how the address field and register values are combined.

The resulting actual memory address is the effective address.
qs.rel: Effective address is the final operand address after applying the addressing mode (A, (A), PC + A, XR + A). Physical address after translation is a separate concept from virtual or logical address.

qs.stem: In which of the following type of addressing mode, the instruction specifies a register in the CPU whose contents give the address of the operand in memory?
qs.sol: In register indirect addressing, the instruction names a CPU register whose contents hold the memory address of the operand.
qs.rel: Register indirect: register holds the memory address of the operand, one memory reference. Compare indirect (memory location holds address, two references) and autoincrement variant used for stepping through arrays.

qs.stem: Machine instructions that involve movement of data in or out of registers and or memory locations belongs to which of the following categories?
qs.sol:
Data movement instructions transfer values between registers and memory or other locations.

Data movement covers transfers into or out of registers and memory.
qs.rel: Instruction categories: data movement (load, store, move, push, pop), data processing (arithmetic and logic), control (branch, call, halt), I/O. Data storage refers to memory, not an instruction class.

qs.stem: With reference to Operating System overview, which of the following defines the repertoire of machine language instructions that a computer can follow?
qs.sol:
The instruction set architecture specifies the machine-language instructions visible to software.

The ISA defines the machine-language operations a processor can execute.
qs.rel: Instruction set architecture is the machine-instruction repertoire visible to software; ABI and API are higher interfaces. Architecture (visible to programmer) vs organisation (hardware implementation) is the classic contrast.

qs.stem: Which field of instruction is used to locate the operands needed for an operation?
qs.sol:
The mode field specifies how the operand location is to be found from the instruction.

The official key selects Mode; an address field alone supplies a value whose interpretation depends on that mode.
qs.rel: Mode field says how to interpret the address field and locate operands; address field gives the address or value; opcode gives the operation. Relate to EA calculation and addressing modes.

qs.stem: In which of the following type of computers do the programs and data often reside in a different memory system?
qs.sol:
Many embedded computers use microcontrollers with separate program and data memories, an arrangement associated with Harvard architecture.

RISC and CISC describe instruction-set design, whereas stored-program describes storing instructions in memory.
qs.rel: Embedded computers often use microcontrollers with separate program memory (ROM/flash) and data memory (RAM), a Harvard-style arrangement. Von Neumann machines share one memory for code and data.

qs.stem: When computers are classified by their role within a larger device, which class commonly uses microcontrollers whose program instructions and runtime data reside in separate memory systems?
qs.sol:
Concept

Computer systems can organize instructions and data in two broad ways. A von Neumann organization uses a shared memory path, whereas a Harvard organization uses separate instruction and data memories or buses.

RISC and CISC classify instruction-set design; stored-program describes how executable instructions are retained. An application-oriented class instead groups computers by the purpose and setting in which they are used.

Application

The stem fixes the classification axis as the computers role within a larger device, then asks which role-based class commonly uses separate program and data memory systems. …
qs.rel: Harvard vs von Neumann architecture. Embedded microcontroller examples: washing machine, car ECU, remote. Harvard allows simultaneous instruction fetch and data access; von Neumann uses one bus and memory.

qs.stem: The CPU exchanges data with memory. For this purpose, which of the following registers specifies the address in memory for the next read or write?
qs.sol:
The memory address register holds the address for a pending memory read or write.

This register supplies the address for the next memory access.
qs.rel: MAR holds address for pending read/write; MBR/MDR holds the data transferred; PC next instruction; IR current instruction. Memory read: MAR <- address, control read, MDR <- data.

qs.stem:
Which of the given options best describes the truthfulness of the following statements?

i) A compiler translates the entire source code line by line.

ii) Computer architecture refers to those attributes of a system which are visible to a programmer.

iii) The Reduced Instruction Set Architecture (RISC) computer organisation reduces the cycles per instruction at the cost of the number of instructions per program to increase the CPU performance.

iv) All the arithmetic and logical processing is performed by the Arithmetic Logic Unit under the supervision of a control unit.
qs.sol:
Concept

A multi-statement true/false item is solved by judging each statement independently against its own governing definition or principle in computer organisation and architecture, and only then combining the four individual verdicts into one pattern to match against the options.

Application

Statement

	

Verdict

	

Reason




i

	

False

	

A compiler translates the source file into target code before execution begins; it does not translate and run the program line by line the way an interpreter does.




ii

	

True

	

Computer architecture covers the attributes of a system that are visible to a programmer, such as the instruction set, addressing modes, and data types. …
qs.rel: Mixed true/false on architecture: compiler translates the whole program (not line by line), architecture means programmer-visible attributes, RISC uses simple instructions and load/store. Judge each statement separately.

qs.stem: Which of the following part of the CPU has the necessary electronic circuitry to perform binary addition and shift operations in computer system?
qs.sol: The ALU performs arithmetic and logic operations, including binary addition and shift operations.
qs.rel: ALU performs addition and shifting using adders and shifters. Registers store, control unit controls, buses transfer. Related: barrel shifter, carry-lookahead, status flags.

qs.stem: The processing required for a single instruction execution by CPU is called _____.
qs.sol:
An instruction cycle comprises the CPU work needed to fetch and execute one instruction.

An instruction cycle spans the processing of one instruction.
qs.rel: Instruction cycle: fetch, decode, execute (plus interrupt check). Machine cycle = memory/I/O access; clock cycle = shortest time unit. Pipelining overlaps instruction cycles.

qs.stem: What is the full form of MISD?

opts.A: Multiple Interrupt stream and Single Data stream
opts.B: Multiple Instruction stream and Single Data stream
opts.C: Many Interrupt stream and Single Digital stream
opts.D: Many Instruction stream and Single Digital stream

qs.sol:
Correct answer: Multiple Instruction stream and Single Data stream

In Flynn’s taxonomy, MISD expands as Multiple Instruction stream, Single Data stream. It describes an architecture where multiple instruction streams operate on the same data stream.

Final answer: Multiple Instruction stream and Single Data stream.
qs.rel: Flynn's taxonomy: SISD (uniprocessor), SIMD (vector, GPU), MISD (rare), MIMD (multiprocessor/multicomputer). Classification by instruction stream and data stream counts.

qs.stem: Which of the following is characteristic of a RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) processor?

opts.B: Instruction that manipulate operands in memory
opts.D: A large number (typically from 100 to 250) of instructions

qs.sol: RISC processors typically use fixed-length, easily decoded instruction formats and a simpler instruction set.
qs.rel: RISC features: fixed-length easily decoded format, hardwired control, load/store, large register file, single-cycle execution. Microprogrammed control and memory operands are CISC traits.

qs.stem: Which of the following in a microprogrammed control unit is a next address generator?
qs.sol:
The microprogram sequencer generates the address of the next microinstruction.

A control address register holds an address but does not generate it.
qs.rel: Microprogram sequencer generates the next microinstruction address (branch, increment, subroutine). Control address register holds the current address; control memory stores microinstructions; pipeline register holds output.

qs.stem: Which of the following microprogrammed control unit organisations does NOT need any decoder circuitry to generate the control signals?
qs.sol:
In horizontal microprogramming, individual control bits directly select control signals.

Thus there is no encoded control field that needs decoding.
qs.rel: Horizontal microcode has one bit per control signal (wide, fast, no decoder). Vertical microcode encodes fields and needs decoders (narrow, slower). Nanoprogramming is a two-level variant.

qs.stem: What happens when branch instruction “BR ADR” is executed?

opts.A: It transfers the value of ADR into IR.
opts.B: It transfers the value of ADR into AC.
opts.C: It transfers the value of ADR into PC.
opts.D: It transfers the value of ADR into MAR.

qs.sol: When the branch instruction BR ADR is executed, the address specified by ADR is loaded directly into the Program Counter (PC). This directs the CPU to fetch subsequent instructions from that new memory location, altering the program flow.
qs.rel: BR ADR is an unconditional branch: PC <- ADR. Conditional branches test flags. CALL saves PC on stack first, RET restores it. Branch targets can be absolute or PC-relative.

topics.deep:
- **CPU registers:** **PC** (address of the NEXT instruction), **IR** (the instruction being executed, used by control unit), **MAR** (address for pending memory read/write), **MDR/MBR** (data to/from memory), **AC** (accumulator), **SP** (address of stack top), **flag/status register (PSW)**, index and base registers, general-purpose registers, I/O buffer register (data exchanged with I/O module).
- **Instruction cycle (fetch-decode-execute):** Fetch: MAR <- PC; MDR <- M[MAR]; PC <- PC + 1; IR <- MDR. Decode: control unit interprets opcode and mode. Execute: operand fetch (if any), ALU operation, result store. An **interrupt check** follows; a **machine cycle** is one memory/I/O access, a **clock cycle (T-state)** is the smallest unit.
- **Architecture vs organisation:** **architecture** = attributes visible to the programmer (instruction set, addressing modes, data types, I/O mechanisms - the **ISA**); **organisation** = operational units and interconnections (control signals, memory technology). Same ISA, different organisation. **Von Neumann** = one memory for program+data; **Harvard** = separate program and data memories (embedded microcontrollers, DSPs).
- **Instruction format fields:** **opcode** (what operation - n bits give **2^n** operations), **address field(s)** (where the operands/result are), **mode field** (how to interpret the address field). Mnemonics are symbolic opcodes. Instruction types: data transfer/movement, arithmetic, logical, shift/rotate, control/branch, I/O.
- **Address count - worked example X = (A+B)*(C+D):**
- **3-address:** ADD R1,A,B; ADD R2,C,D; MUL X,R1,R2 (short programs, long instructions).
- **2-address:** MOV R1,A; ADD R1,B; MOV R2,C; ADD R2,D; MUL R1,R2; MOV X,R1 (one operand is also the destination).
- **1-address (accumulator):** LOAD A; ADD B; STORE T; LOAD C; ADD D; MUL T; STORE X (AC is implicit).
- **0-address (stack):** PUSH A; PUSH B; ADD; PUSH C; PUSH D; ADD; MUL; POP X (operands implicit on top of stack, postfix/reverse Polish: AB+CD+*).
- **Stack:** LIFO; SP holds address of top; PUSH: SP <- SP - 1, M[SP] <- data; POP: data <- M[SP], SP <- SP + 1 (stack grows downward in typical layouts). Used for subroutine calls, interrupts, expression evaluation.
- **Addressing modes (EA = effective address):**

| Mode | Operand / EA | Memory refs for operand |
|---|---|---|
| Implied | operand implicit (AC, SP, complement) | 0 |
| Immediate | operand = A in instruction | 0 |
| Register | operand in register R | 0 |
| Register indirect | EA = (R) | 1 |
| Direct (absolute) | EA = A | 1 |
| Indirect | EA = (A) | 2 |
| Relative | EA = PC + A (position-independent code, branches) | 1 |
| Indexed | EA = XR + A (arrays) | 1 |
| Base register | EA = BR + A (relocation) | 1 |
| Auto-increment/decrement | EA = (R), then R changes | 1 |

- **Displacement** family (relative, indexed, base) all use EA = A + (R). **One mode bit** distinguishes direct vs indirect. **Effective address** = the final memory address after the mode computation.
- **Addressable units:** byte-addressable memory with A address bits has **2^A** locations.
- **RISC vs CISC:**

| Feature | RISC | CISC |
|---|---|---|
| Instruction set | small, simple | large, complex |
| Length | fixed, easily decoded | variable |
| Addressing modes | few | many |
| Execution | mostly single cycle, pipelined | multi-cycle |
| Memory access | only LOAD/STORE | any instruction |
| Control | hardwired | microprogrammed |
| Registers | large register file | fewer |
| Examples | ARM, MIPS, SPARC | Intel x86, VAX |

- **Control unit:** **hardwired** (gates, fast, inflexible) vs **microprogrammed** (control memory/store, a ROM holding **microinstructions**; a set of microinstructions = microprogram). Control address register (CAR) holds the next microinstruction address; the **sequencer (next-address generator)** computes it. A **control word** is the set of control bits for micro-operations. **Horizontal** microinstruction: wide, one bit per control signal, no decoder, fast, parallel. **Vertical**: encoded fields, needs decoders, narrow, slower.
- **Branch:** BR ADR loads ADR into **PC** (unconditional); conditional branches test flags (Z, C, S, V). CALL pushes PC; RET pops it.
- **Flynn's taxonomy:** **SISD** (conventional), **SIMD** (vector/array processors, GPUs), **MISD** (rare, fault tolerant), **MIMD** (multiprocessors).
- **Pipelining:** overlapping instruction stages; ideal speedup for k stages and n tasks = n*k / (k + n - 1). Hazards: structural, data (RAW), control (branch).
- **Memory hierarchy link:** only main memory and cache communicate directly with CPU; RAM is volatile and random access.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) which register holds SP/flags/current instruction/data from memory; (2) number of memory accesses for a given addressing mode; (3) EA calculation numeric problem (EA = A + index); (4) count opcode bits given number of instructions; (5) classify a given instruction as 0/1/2/3-address; (6) convert infix to postfix and write stack code; (7) RISC vs CISC match; (8) horizontal vs vertical microprogramming; (9) steps of fetch cycle in micro-operations; (10) Flynn's classification examples.

topics.title: 3. Assembly Language & the 8085 Microprocessor
topics.theory:
- **Assembly vs machine language:** machine language = binary, machine dependent, hard to modify; assembly uses **mnemonics**, translated by an **assembler** (**pseudo-instructions/directives are for the assembler**, e.g. ORG, END, EQU); **macro** invoked by its name (not CALL/JMP). **Comment symbol in 8085 assembly: `;`**. User-defined tokens = labels/names (e.g. ABC; A, SP, PSW are reserved registers). **END directive** tells the assembler the program ends.
- **8085 (8-bit):** **MVI A, 32H** = move immediate (2-byte instruction, loads 32H into A); **MOV A, B** = register copy (1 byte); **LDA addr** = load accumulator from memory address (3 bytes); **ADD B** adds B to A (1 byte, result in A); **ADI data** = add immediate 8-bit data to accumulator (2 bytes); **JMP addr** = jump to new program location; STA, LXI, PUSH, POP, CALL, RET. Registers A, B, C, D, E, H, L, SP, PC, flags (S, Z, AC, P, CY). 16-bit address bus → 64 KB.
- **Accumulator-based evaluation of Y = (A−B)/(C+D×E):** LOAD D, MUL E, ADD C, STORE T, LOAD A, SUB B, DIV T, STORE Y.

qs.stem: Which of the following is the assembly language instruction for ‘Jump to new program location’?
qs.sol:
JMP transfers control directly to the supplied program address.

This instruction jumps to the specified program address.
qs.rel: JMP is the unconditional jump; conditional jumps JZ, JNZ, JC, JNC test flags. In 8085 JMP is 3 bytes (opcode C3H plus 16-bit address). CALL and RET manage subroutines; PCHL jumps to HL contents.

qs.stem: Pseudo instruction is given to ______.
qs.sol: Pseudo instructions are special commands used in assembly language that do not translate directly into machine code. Instead, they are processed by the assembler during translation to handle tasks like memory allocation or data definition.
qs.rel: Pseudo-instructions (directives) like ORG, END, EQU, DB are instructions to the assembler; they produce no machine opcode. Contrast with real instructions (MOV, ADD) and macros (text expansion).

qs.stem: Which of the following languages is a low-level programming language that is intended to directly communicate with a computer's hardware and to be readable by humans?
qs.sol:
Assembly language uses human-readable mnemonics that map closely to hardware instructions.

Assembly uses readable symbols to express hardware-level instructions.
qs.rel: Assembly is a low-level, machine-dependent language using mnemonics, translated by an assembler. Binary and hexadecimal are machine-code representations. Compare with high-level languages needing compilers.

qs.stem: Opcodes are represented by abbreviations called:
qs.sol:
Opcodes in assembly language are represented using mnemonics, which are short, human-readable abbreviations of machine instructions.
Examples:

ADD → Addition

SUB → Subtraction

MOV → Move data

These make programming easier compared to writing binary codes directly.
qs.rel: Opcodes are written as mnemonics (MOV, ADD, JMP). The assembler maps mnemonic to binary opcode. Lexemes are lexical units in compilers; operators act in high-level expressions.

qs.stem: Which of the following in assembly language is entered into the operation code for each assemble program instruction to specify a shortened "opcode" that represents a larger, complete set of codes?
qs.sol:
A mnemonic is a shortened symbolic operation name used in assembly source to stand for an opcode.

A mnemonic is the short symbolic name for a machine operation.
qs.rel: Mnemonic = symbolic opcode name; label = symbolic address; directive = assembler command; macro = named code block. Know the four assembly source elements: label, mnemonic, operand, comment.

qs.stem: Which of the following symbols is used to write a comment in assembly program?
qs.sol: In assembly programming, the semicolon symbol (;) is used to denote comments. Any text following a semicolon on a line is ignored by the assembler and does not affect program execution.
qs.rel: Assembly comments begin with ; in 8085/x86 assemblers. Comments are ignored by the assembler. Labels end with a colon in 8085 syntax.

qs.stem: Which of the following is false regarding the machine language?

opts.C: It is made up of 1’s and 0’s

qs.sol: It is easier to modify
qs.rel: Machine language is binary, machine dependent, hard to program and modify; assembly eases this with mnemonics. First generation languages = machine; second = assembly; third = high-level.

qs.stem: What is the meaning of assembly language instruction 'LDA (Address)'?
qs.sol:
LDA loads the accumulator from the memory location identified by the address operand.

The accumulator receives the contents of the addressed memory location.
qs.rel: LDA addr loads accumulator from the memory address (3 bytes, direct addressing). STA stores A to memory; LDAX loads via BC/DE; LHLD loads HL pair; MVI loads an immediate value.

qs.stem: Which of the following is a user defined token in 8080/8085 assembly language?
qs.sol: In 8085 assembly, registers like A and SP are predefined system tokens. User-defined tokens include labels or identifiers created by the programmer, such as ABC. Therefore, ABC is the correct user-defined token among the choices provided.
qs.rel: User-defined tokens are labels and names; registers (A, B, SP, PSW) and mnemonics are reserved words. Labels in 8085 have up to 6 characters and cannot be reserved words.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are true about "MVI A, 32H" instruction of the 8085? 
(i) It is a 2-byte instruction. 
(ii) It moves the hexadecimal data 32H in the accumulator.
qs.sol: The MVI A, 32H instruction requires two bytes: one for the opcode and one for the immediate data. It specifically loads the hexadecimal value 32H into the accumulator register A. Thus, both provided statements accurately describe this operation.
qs.rel: MVI A,32H is a 2-byte immediate-data instruction (opcode 3EH + data) that loads 32H into A with no flag change. LXI is 3 bytes; MOV is 1 byte. Count bytes = opcode + operand bytes.

qs.stem: Which of the following is the operation of the ADI instruction of the 8085?

opts.A: Add immediate 8 bits data to Program Counter (PC).
opts.C: Add immediate 8 bits data to accumulator.
opts.D: Add register data to Program Counter (PC).

qs.sol: The ADI instruction in the 8085 microprocessor stands for Add Immediate. It adds an immediate 8-bit operand directly to the contents of the accumulator register.
qs.rel: ADI adds 8-bit immediate data to A (2 bytes, opcode C6H) and affects all flags. ADD r adds a register; ACI adds with carry; SUI subtracts immediate. Result always stays in A.

qs.stem: In assembly, how is a macro invoked after its definition?

opts.C: By writing its name followed by MACRO
opts.D: By simply writing its name with any required parameters

qs.sol:
Concept

An assembler macro is a named template of assembly-source statements. Macro processing happens during assembly: arguments replace formal parameters, and the expanded statements are then assembled.

Defining a template and invoking it are separate operations. Runtime branch and subroutine instructions instead control execution of the generated machine code.

Application

For a MASM-style example, define a macro with one parameter:

LOADVAL MACRO value
    MOV AX, value
ENDM

The definition records LOADVAL as the macro name and value as its formal parameter; it does not invoke the template.

The source statement LOADVAL 7 invokes the template with actual argument 7. …
qs.rel: Macro invocation: write the macro name (with arguments) in the code; the assembler expands it inline. Subroutines use CALL. Macro definition is delimited by MACRO and ENDM.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about "MOV A, B" instruction of the 8085?

opts.C: Its right most 7 bit represents the operand B.
opts.D: Its addressing mode is "Register address mode".

qs.sol:
The MOV A, B instruction is a single-byte operation with opcode 46H. It uses Register Addressing Mode as both operands are CPU registers, validating Option 4.

⚠ Correction: the opcode of MOV A,B is 78H (binary 01 111 000: destination A = 111, source B = 000) — 46H is MOV B,M. The answer D (register addressing) is still right.
qs.rel: MOV A,B is a 1-byte register-addressing instruction copying B to A (opcode 78H, from 01 DDD SSS with A = 111, B = 000). MOV r,M uses HL-addressed memory. Data transfer does not affect flags.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about "ADD B" instruction of the 8085?

opts.A: It is used to add the content of register B to Accumulator.
opts.C: Its operand is B whose code is 101.

qs.sol:
The ADD B instruction adds the contents of Register B to the Accumulator using opcode 80H. Option C is factually incorrect because Register B's internal code is 000, not 101. Since the question asks for the incorrect statement, Option C is the correct selection.

⚠ Correction: ADD B = 80H (10 000 000); register codes are B=000, C=001, D=010, E=011, H=100, L=101, M=110, A=111. Option C (B = 101) is wrong because 101 is L.
qs.rel: ADD B is one byte, opcode 80H (10000 SSS), register B code = 000; sum goes to A and all flags are updated. ADD M adds memory at HL; ADC adds carry too.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about END directive of the 8080/8085 assembly language?

opts.A: It specifies the end of the assembly program.
opts.B: In an assembly program, there may be more than one END directive.
opts.C: END directive may have optional expression operand.
opts.D: If END directive exists without expression operand, then assembler assumes zero as the starting address for program execution.

qs.sol: The END directive marks the logical end of an assembly program and must occur exactly once. While specifying a start address is optional, claiming multiple END directives are permitted violates standard 8085 assembler rules.
qs.rel: END directive appears exactly once and tells the assembler to stop translating. ORG sets starting address, EQU assigns a value, DB/DW define data. Code after END is ignored.

qs.stem: Which sequence of one-address, accumulator-based instructions can be used to evaluate Y = (A - B) / (C + D * E)?

opts.A:
LOAD D
MPY E
ADD C
STORE Y
LOAD A
SUB B
DIV Y
STORE Y
opts.B:
LOAD D
MPY E
ADD C
LOAD A
STORE Y
SUB B
DIV Y
STORE Y
opts.C:
LOAD D
ADD C
MPY E
STORE Y
LOAD A
SUB B
DIV Y
STORE Y
opts.D:
LOAD D
MPY E
ADD C
STORE Y
LOAD A
DIV Y
SUB B
STORE Y

qs.sol:
Instruction logic:

Denominator: First compute D * E, then add C to get C + D * E. Store this intermediate value.

Numerator: Then compute A - B.

Final division: Divide the numerator by the stored denominator and store the result in Y.

Correct sequence:

LOAD D
MPY E
ADD C
STORE Y
LOAD A
SUB B
DIV Y
STORE Y

Final answer: Option A
qs.rel: One-address accumulator code: evaluate denominator first (LOAD D, MPY E, ADD C), store in temporary, then numerator and DIV. Expression order must respect precedence; temporaries are needed since only one AC exists.

topics.deep:
- **Language levels:** machine language (binary, machine dependent, fastest, hard to write/modify) < **assembly language** (mnemonics, one-to-one with machine code, machine dependent, translated by an **assembler**) < high-level language (compiler/interpreter, portable). Assembly is a low-level, symbolic language close to hardware.
- **Assembler:** usually **two-pass** - pass 1 builds the symbol table (labels to addresses), pass 2 generates machine code. **Pseudo-instructions / directives** are commands to the assembler, not translated to opcodes: **ORG** (set origin), **END** (end of program, used once), **EQU** (define constant), **DB/DW** (define byte/word), DS (reserve space). **Mnemonic** = abbreviation of an opcode (MOV, ADD). **Label** = symbolic address. **Comment** begins with **;**.
- **Macro vs subroutine:** a macro is a named block of source text expanded **inline** wherever its name is written (no CALL, no JMP); a subroutine exists once and is reached with CALL/RET. Macro = faster but bigger code.
- **8085 basics:** 8-bit microprocessor (data bus 8 bits), **16-bit address bus -> 64 KB** memory, 40-pin, +5 V single supply, on-chip clock generator, 3 MHz. Lower address lines multiplexed with data (AD0-AD7), ALE latches low byte. 8086 is 16-bit (20-bit address, 1 MB); 80386 is 32-bit.
- **Registers:** A (accumulator), B, C, D, E, H, L (8-bit); pairs **BC, DE, HL**; **M** = memory location addressed by HL; SP and PC are 16 bits. Register codes: B=000, C=001, D=010, E=011, H=100, L=101, M=110, A=111.
- **Flags (5):** **S** (sign, D7), **Z** (zero, D6), **AC** (auxiliary carry, D4), **P** (parity, D2), **CY** (carry, D0).
- **Addressing modes:** immediate (MVI A,32H), register (MOV A,B), direct (LDA 2050H), register indirect (MOV A,M; LDAX B) and implied (CMA, RAL).
- **Instruction groups with sizes:**

| Group | Examples | Bytes | Flags |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data transfer | MOV r,r (1); MVI r,data (2); LXI rp,16-bit (3); LDA/STA addr (3); LHLD/SHLD (3); LDAX/STAX (1); XCHG (1) | 1-3 | none affected |
| Arithmetic | ADD r, ADC, SUB, SBB (1); ADI, ACI, SUI, SBI (2); INR/DCR (1); INX/DCX (1); DAD rp (1); DAA | 1-2 | all five; INR/DCR do not touch CY; INX/DCX none; DAD only CY |
| Logical | ANA, ORA, XRA, CMP (1); ANI, ORI, XRI, CPI (2); RLC, RRC, RAL, RAR, CMA, CMC, STC (1) | 1-2 | ANA sets AC=1, CY=0; ORA/XRA reset CY, AC; CMA none |
| Branch | JMP addr, JZ, JNZ, JC, JNC, CALL (3); RET, PCHL (1); RST n (1) | 1-3 | none |
| Stack, I/O, machine control | PUSH, POP, XTHL, SPHL (1); IN/OUT port (2); NOP, HLT, EI, DI, RIM, SIM (1) | 1-2 | POP PSW restores flags |

- **Encoding:** MOV r1,r2 = 01 DDD SSS, so **MOV A,B = 78H**; ADD r = 10000 SSS, so **ADD B = 80H** (B = 000); MVI A,data = 3EH; LDA = 3AH; STA = 32H; JMP = C3H; ADI = C6H; NOP = 00H; HLT = 76H.
- **CMP:** A = operand sets Z=1; A < operand sets CY=1. Used before JZ/JNC.
- **T-states (typical):** MOV r,r = 4; MVI r = 7; LDA/STA = 13; ADD r = 4; JMP = 10; CALL = 18; RET = 10; PUSH = 12; POP = 10; HLT = 5.
- **Interrupts:** TRAP (non-maskable, highest priority), RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5 (maskable, vectored), INTR (non-vectored, external RST/CALL supplied). EI/DI enable/disable; SIM sets masks; RIM reads them. Serial lines SID/SOD.
- **I/O:** IN/OUT use an 8-bit port address (256 ports, I/O-mapped); memory-mapped I/O uses 16-bit memory addresses with ordinary LDA/STA.
- **Sample program (add 2 bytes):** LDA 2050H; MOV B,A; LDA 2051H; ADD B; STA 2052H; HLT.
- **Accumulator-based expression Y = (A-B)/(C+D*E):** LOAD D; MPY E; ADD C; STORE T; LOAD A; SUB B; DIV T; STORE Y. Rule: evaluate the denominator first and save to a temporary, since a one-address machine has only one accumulator.
- **Loop idiom:** MVI C,count; LOOP: ...; DCR C; JNZ LOOP (Z flag decides).
- **Likely question angles:** (1) number of bytes in a given 8085 instruction (LXI, STA, ADI, MOV); (2) which flags a given instruction affects; (3) hex opcode of MOV/ADD/MVI; (4) result in A after a short MVI/ADI/ANA program; (5) which interrupt has highest priority or is non-maskable; (6) difference between directive and instruction; (7) macro vs subroutine; (8) number of flags and their names; (9) size of address bus and memory addressed by 8085; (10) output after CMP for a given pair of values.

topics.title: 4. Memory — RAM, ROM, Cache, Disk & Storage
topics.theory:
- **Memory hierarchy (fast→slow, small→large):** registers → cache → main memory (RAM) → secondary (disk, tape) → tertiary. **Only main memory (primary) and cache communicate directly with the CPU.** Auxiliary/tertiary memory do not.
- **RAM** = Random Access Memory (volatile, read/write; any location same time). **SRAM** cell = **flip-flops**, faster, costlier, used for cache; **DRAM** = capacitors (needs refresh), cheaper, main memory. **Three forms typically volatile & semiconductor:** SRAM, DRAM (RAM family). ROM/PROM/EPROM/EEPROM/Flash = non-volatile. **DIMM (Dual Inline Memory Module)** = PCB with DRAM chips mounted on both sides. **Random-access** = access time constant regardless of location; sequential (tape), direct (disk).
- **Cache mapping:** **direct**, **associative**, **set-associative**; direct mapping maps each main-memory block into **exactly one** possible cache line. **Write policies:** **write-through** (update both) vs **write-back** (only cache updated during write; main memory updated on replacement).
- **Addressing arithmetic:** n address lines → **2ⁿ** locations (10 lines → 1024; 16 lines → 64K; 2K×16 memory → **11 address lines, 16 data lines**; 64K×8 → 16 address, 8 data lines). Chips needed = total capacity ÷ chip capacity (128K×8 bits ÷ 16K×1 = **64 chips**). A 16 KB memory decodes using higher address lines (A0–A13 select within chip, A14–A15 decode).
- **Magnetic disk:** surfaces → **tracks → sectors → cylinders**; **seek time** (head to track) + **rotational latency** (wait for the sector under head) + transfer time. **Magnetic tape:** sequential access, large capacity, cheap, not direct access. Hard disk can serve as virtual-memory extension. **Unit of transfer:** main memory = number of bits read/written at a time (word), external = block.

qs.stem: Unicode in the programming language can be represented using which of the bit format standards in computer science?
qs.sol: Unicode characters are commonly represented through UTF-8, an 8-bit based encoding standard. Among the listed options, 8-bit is the intended answer.
qs.rel: Unicode encodings: UTF-8 (variable 1-4 bytes), UTF-16 (2 or 4 bytes), UTF-32 (fixed 4 bytes). ASCII is 7-bit with 128 symbols; extended ASCII 8-bit. Unicode supports all languages including Hindi.

qs.stem:
Identify the valid cache organization techniques: 
(i) Direct
(ii) Associative 
(iii) Set-associative
qs.sol:
Cache mapping technique is the rule that decides which cache line (or lines) a given block of main memory is allowed to occupy. Computer architecture recognizes exactly three such techniques: direct mapping (each block maps to exactly one specific line, found from the block address), (fully) associative mapping (a block may be placed in any line, so every line's tag must be compared to locate it), and set-associative mapping (the cache is divided into sets; a block maps to one specific set but can occupy any line within that set, combining the previous two ideas).

The stem lists exactly these three schemes as (i) Direct, (ii) Associative, and (iii) Set-associative. …
qs.rel: Cache mapping: direct, fully associative, set-associative. Direct is simplest with conflict misses; associative is flexible but costly. Cache sits between CPU and main memory and exploits locality.

qs.stem: A cell of the SRAM is made with ______.
qs.sol: SRAM (Static Random Access Memory) cells are constructed using flip-flop circuits, specifically a latch configuration made of cross-coupled inverters. This design allows the cell to maintain its stored data state as long as power is supplied, without needing periodic refreshing. A standard SRAM bit cell typically uses six transistors to form this stable latch, ensuring fast access times and high reliability. In contrast, DRAM (Dynamic Random Access Memory) cells store data using capacitors that leak charge over time and require refreshing. Magnetic dipoles or magnetic cores are associated with older technologies like magnetic core memory or modern MRAM, not standard SRAM. …
qs.rel: SRAM cell uses flip-flops (about six transistors), needs no refresh, is fast, costly and used for cache. DRAM uses capacitors and needs refresh. Core memory used magnetic cores; ROM cells are fuses or transistors.

qs.stem: What is a key difference between system software and application software?

opts.A: System software includes programs like web browsers, while application software includes operating systems.
opts.B: System software is designed for end-users, while application software is designed for system administrators only.
opts.C: System software operates the computer hardware, whereas application software is designed to perform specific user-oriented tasks.
opts.D: System software is optional for computer operation, while application software is mandatory.

qs.sol:
System software supplies the operating environment: it allocates memory, controls devices and provides services that programs use. Operating systems and device drivers belong to this category.

Application software uses those services to carry out user tasks such as browsing, editing documents or processing accounts. Comparing the two roles identifies hardware operation versus specific user-oriented tasks as the distinction.
qs.rel: System software supports operation of the computer and runs other programs; application software serves end-user tasks. Examples: OS and compilers vs word processor and spreadsheet. Utility software is in between.

qs.stem: Which of the following does the actual display in a computer?
qs.sol: CRT stands for Cathode Ray Tube, an older display technology used to actually display output on a computer monitor.
qs.rel: Display chain: CPU/GPU computes image, VRAM holds frame buffer, monitor (CRT, LCD, LED) shows it. Resolution, refresh rate, pixel and dot pitch are display terms.

qs.stem: A disk consists of ____ , ____ , ____ .
qs.sol:
Option 4: cylinder, tracks and sectors

In computer storage architecture, a hard disk drive is organized into a specific geometric hierarchy:

Tracks: Concentric circles on the surface of a disk platter.

Sectors: Small segments that each track is divided into (typically the smallest unit of data that can be read or written).

Cylinders: A set of tracks at the same distance from the center across all platter surfaces.
qs.rel: Hard disk organisation: platters, surfaces, tracks (concentric), sectors (arcs), and cylinders (same track on all surfaces). Capacity = surfaces x tracks x sectors x bytes per sector.

qs.stem: When n bits are used to represent an operation (op) code, then how many different operations a computer can perform?
qs.sol: When n bits are used to represent an operation code, each bit can be either 0 or 1. The total number of unique combinations is 2 raised to the power of n, or 2ⁿ. This is because each bit doubles the number of possible codes. For example, with 1 bit, there are 2 codes (0 and 1); with 2 bits, there are 4 codes (00, 01, 10, 11), and so on. Therefore, the number of different operations a computer can perform is 2ⁿ.
qs.rel: n-bit opcode allows 2^n distinct operations; conversely m operations need ceil(log2 m) bits. Instruction length = opcode + mode + address fields.

qs.stem: How many bits are required to distinguish between a direct and an indirect address?
qs.sol: To distinguish between two mutually exclusive addressing modes, only one binary digit is necessary. This single bit can encode the two distinct states required for direct and indirect addressing within standard instruction sets.
qs.rel: Number of mode bits needed: 1 bit distinguishes two modes; 2 bits for up to 4 modes (k bits give 2^k modes). Mano's basic computer uses one bit I for direct/indirect.

qs.stem: With respect to size, which of the following represents the correct relationships between different categories of cache memory?
qs.sol: In computer architecture, cache memory sizes increase as we move down the hierarchy. Level 1 (L1) cache is the smallest and fastest, while Level 2 (L2) and Level 3 (L3) caches are progressively larger but slower. Therefore, the correct size relationship is L1 < L2 < L3.
qs.rel: Cache hierarchy: L1 smallest and fastest, per core; L2 larger; L3 largest and shared. Access time and size increase down the levels; all are SRAM, main memory is DRAM.

qs.stem: Which of the following memory access methods in a computer system involves referring to any location that can be selected at random and directly addressed and accessed?
qs.sol:
Random access selects any addressed location directly, without traversing earlier locations.

Random access permits direct selection of an arbitrary address.
qs.rel: Random access: any location selected directly in constant time (RAM, ROM). Sequential (tape) and direct (disk) are different. Associative memory searches by content.

qs.stem: With respect to cache organisation, direct mapping maps each block of main memory into ________ possible cache line.
qs.sol: In direct mapping, each block of main memory maps to exactly one specific cache line. This differs from set-associative or fully associative mapping where multiple lines are possible.
qs.rel: Direct mapping: line = block number mod number of lines; each block maps to exactly one line. Address split into tag, line index, word offset. Set-associative maps a block to one set but any line in it.

qs.stem: In which of the following cache write methods for updating main memory, only cache location is updated during write operation?
qs.sol:
Write-back updates the cache line first and writes main memory later, usually on eviction.

Write-through updates main memory during the write.
qs.rel: Write-back updates only cache and sets a dirty bit; memory is updated when the line is replaced. Write-through updates both. Write-back reduces bus traffic but complicates coherence.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements about DRAM memory is correct?

opts.A: It stands for Data Random Access Memory.
opts.D: Its cells are usually made with capacitors.

qs.sol: Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) stores data in capacitors that leak charge over time. This requires periodic refreshing to maintain data integrity, unlike Static RAM which uses flip-flops. Additionally, DRAM is generally slower and denser compared to SRAM technology.
qs.rel: DRAM stores bits as capacitor charge, needs periodic refresh, is slower and cheaper than SRAM, and is used as main memory. SDRAM, DDR are synchronous variants.

qs.stem:
Select the option that best describes the truthfulness of the following statements.

i) RAM is volatile memory and generally has less storage capacity than secondary-storage devices.

ii) Secondary memory is auxiliary storage outside primary memory; RAM and ROM are examples of primary memory.
qs.sol:
Concept

Volatility tells us whether stored data survives when power is removed, while storage capacity tells us how much data a device can hold. In the standard memory classification, RAM and ROM are primary memory; secondary memory is non-volatile auxiliary storage, such as an HDD or SSD, outside primary memory.

Application

For statement i, RAM requires continuous power to retain its contents, so it is volatile. Its capacity is also limited relative to mass-storage devices such as HDDs and SSDs. Therefore, statement i is true.

For statement ii, secondary memory means auxiliary storage outside primary memory. …
qs.rel: Volatile memory loses content without power (RAM, cache, registers). Primary memory = RAM and ROM; secondary = HDD, SSD, tape, optical. Secondary memory has larger capacity and is non-volatile.

Which of the following statement(s) is/are NOT true about magnetic tapes?
 I. Direct access device

qs.sol: Only I
qs.rel: Magnetic tape is sequential access, high capacity, cheap, used for backup and archival; it is not a direct-access device. Disk is direct access. Tape records are read in order, so access is slow.

qs.stem:
Arrange the following memory units in descending order.
 Gigabyte, Megabyte, Exabyte, Zettabyte, Petabyte, Yottabyte

opts.A: Yottabyte, Zettabyte, Exabyte, Petabyte, Gigabyte, Megabyte
opts.B: Zettabyte, Yottabyte, Petabyte, Exabyte, Megabyte, Gigabyte

opts.D: Zettabyte, Petabyte, Yottabyte, Exabyte, Gigabyte, Megabyte

qs.sol:
To arrange the memory units in descending order, recall the standard binary prefixes used for digital storage:

The units in ascending order are: Megabyte (MB), Gigabyte (GB), Terabyte (TB), Petabyte (PB), Exabyte (EB), Zettabyte (ZB), Yottabyte (YB).

Therefore, in descending order, the sequence is: Yottabyte, Zettabyte, Exabyte, Petabyte, Gigabyte, Megabyte.

Each unit is 1024 times larger than the previous one, so the order is based on increasing magnitude.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statements is correct?

(i) A hard disk is also used to provide an extension to the main memory known as virtual memory.
(ii) DRAM is faster than SRAM.
(iii) External, nonvolatile memory is also referred to as 'secondary memory' or 'auxiliary memory'.
qs.sol: Statement (i) is correct because virtual memory uses hard disk space to extend main memory capacity. Statement (ii) is incorrect since SRAM operates faster than DRAM due to its static design. Statement (iii) is accurate as external nonvolatile storage is commonly termed secondary or auxiliary memory.
qs.rel: Virtual memory uses hard disk to extend main memory; SRAM is faster than DRAM; secondary/auxiliary memory is external non-volatile. Cache speeds up memory, virtual memory gives larger address space.

qs.stem: Which of the following refers to a memory access mechanism in which the time to access a given location is constant and independent of the sequence of prior accesses?
qs.sol: The question defines a memory access mechanism where retrieval time remains constant regardless of the sequence of prior accesses. This characteristic is the fundamental definition of Random Access, distinguishing it from sequential methods.
qs.rel: Random access means constant access time independent of previous accesses. Contrast sequential (tape), direct (disk) and associative (content-addressed) access. Access time vs cycle time vs transfer rate are performance terms.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements with reference to serial and parallel devices is FALSE?

opts.A: Serial Transmission has two subclasses synchronous and asynchronous.
opts.B: In Parallel Transmission, various bits are sent together simultaneously with a single clock pulse.
opts.C: The installation and troubleshooting are difficult in parallel transmission system due to its placement in a single physical cable.
opts.D: Parallel Transmission uses a 25-pin port having 17 signal lines and 8 ground lines.

qs.sol:
The paper marks the statement about difficult installation due to placement in a single physical cable as false; that description fits serial cabling rather than parallel transmission.

The cable-placement rationale is misapplied to parallel transmission.
qs.rel: Serial vs parallel transmission: serial sends one bit at a time (synchronous or asynchronous), suits long distance; parallel sends many bits at once over multiple wires and needs more cabling. Check which statement mismatches.

qs.stem: How many 16 K × 1 bit RAM chips are needed to provide a memory capacity of 128 K × 1 byte?
qs.sol:
Concept

A memory module has two independent dimensions: address depth and word width. The number of chips is the depth-expansion factor multiplied by the width-expansion factor.

For a target of Dₜ × Wₜ built from D꜀ × W꜀ chips, the chip count is (Dₜ ÷ D꜀) × (Wₜ ÷ W꜀), provided both ratios are whole numbers.

Application

Depth expansion: 128 K ÷ 16 K = 8 banks, because each bank covers 16 K addresses.

Width expansion: 1 byte = 8 bits, so each bank needs 8 one-bit chips in parallel.

Combine the independent factors: 8 banks × 8 chips per bank = 64 chips.

Therefore, the required memory organization uses 64 RAM chips.

Cross-check

The target stores 128 K × 8 = 1024 K bits. …
qs.rel: Chip count = total capacity / chip capacity. 128K x 8 bits = 1024 Kbits; each chip 16 Kbits; 64 chips. First match width (8 chips wide), then depth (8 deep) when chips are 16K x 1.

qs.stem: The number of addressable memory units for a 10-bit size address bus is:
qs.sol: An n-bit address bus identifies 2^n memory locations. For a 10-bit bus, calculate 2 to the power of 10. This equals 1024 distinct addresses available for memory access.
qs.rel: n-bit address bus selects 2^n locations: 10 bits = 1024, 16 bits = 65536, 32 bits = 4 GB. Data bus width sets word size; address bus width sets memory size.
